title: Xuanzang crosses the desert
hookLine: a monk goes west alone, against an imperial ban, and loses his water in the sand

lines: A WATER BAG SPILLS INTO THE SAND.
cards: The sand drinks it in seconds: a full leather water bag, tipped from a tired hand.
In his biography, that's the moment the monk Xuanzang finds himself beyond China's western border with no water and a long way still to go. He isn't supposed to be there.
The government had forbidden travel out of the country, and he left anyway, slipping past the watchtowers at night.
He was going to India for Buddhist texts, whole and in their own language, so he could stop guessing at what the Chinese versions meant.

teach.b: First, why he went. Xuanzang was a young monk who had studied with teachers across China, and the teachers didn't agree. Neither did the translations he had.
He wanted the source. Second, how he left.
He asked for permission to travel and was refused. He went anyway. His biography, written by his disciple Huili, says a guide set out with him, then lost his nerve and turned back.
An old man traded him a thin red horse that, the old man said, had made the crossing many times. So Xuanzang went on alone, with a horse that knew the way better than he did.
Third, the water. After the bag spilled, he did the sensible thing: he turned back east, toward the last watchtower. Then he stopped.
The biography says he remembered a vow he had made: not to take one step back toward the east until he reached India.
He turned the horse west again.
For days he went without water, until he lay down in the sand. Tradition says he called on Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, and recited the Heart Sutra.
In the night a cool wind woke him, and the old horse pulled toward a patch of grass and a pool. Fourth, what the story is about. It isn't about having no fear.
He was afraid enough to turn around. The brave part was small. Courage can be that size: one turn of the reins, back toward where you meant to go.

how: Chinese Buddhists remember Xuanzang as a model pilgrim and translator, and his journey to India is retold in stories and plays.

games.q: you're Xuanzang. your water is gone, the desert runs on ahead, and the last watchtower behind you has water. what do you do?
o: ride back to the watchtower for water.
turn the horse west again and keep going.
stay where you are and wait for a caravan.
games.why: he did start back east. then he remembered his vow not to take one step east before reaching India, and turned west. days later, the old horse found grass and a pool.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been avoiding because it scares you a little: a phone call, an apology, a question you haven't asked.

Don't solve it; just find the first step, the size of one footprint in sand, and if fear shows up, notice where it sits in the body and breathe there. Then come back to the breath, one and then the next.

wordCard.voice: Xuanzang. The monk who left without permission, lost his water in the desert, turned back, and then turned west again.
